scenes.heading: Snowflake Architecture
scenes.narration: Snowflake's defining idea is separating storage from compute across three cleanly decoupled layers.

scenes.heading: The three layers
bullets: Cloud services: the brain that handles auth, metadata, and query optimization.
Compute: independent virtual warehouses that execute queries.
Storage: compressed columnar data held once in cloud object storage.
Each layer scales on its own without disturbing the others.
scenes.narration: The cloud services layer coordinates authentication, metadata, and query planning. Compute happens in virtual warehouses that you can size and spin up independently. Underneath, all data lives once in centralized columnar storage, so every warehouse reads the same copy.

scenes.heading: The life of a query
scenes.narration: When a query arrives, the services layer parses and optimizes it using rich metadata. It then assigns the work to a virtual warehouse, which scans storage and computes the answer. Results and metadata are cached so repeated queries can return almost instantly.

scenes.heading: Coupled vs decoupled compute
scenes.narration: In older MPP systems storage and compute grow together, so scaling one forces you to pay for the other. Snowflake separates them, letting many warehouses read shared storage at once. That isolation means a heavy load job cannot slow down your dashboards.

scenes.text: Snowflake decouples services, compute, and storage so each scales independently and workloads never collide.
scenes.narration: The separation of services, compute, and storage is what gives Snowflake its elasticity and workload isolation.
